It says to use an approved product at its labelled rate and to wear gloves and cover your mouth and nose, and it does not give you a number out of a bag. Mixing two products out of two bags is making a different product from one, which is one you can neither tell you, and there is no way to know the strength of a mixed product. What the label gives you is the product, the date it is good, the carrier and the product's effect on the crop, and it gives no strength to a mix. Take the product to ICAT and give them the name, and let them name the mix.

No, and a mix is not what the label says. What the ITRA and ICAT brochure says is to use the approved product at its labelled rate in a container no larger than the flower bowl, and to check the current product before any mixing. From the list it names: an approved insecticide, the products named in the 2016 one: flambé for pod protection, an approved fungicide, the products not named and hence unspecified. That is the point, because the label is the rule and the strength is the instruction. If a mix would leave a product bigger than the container, it leaves too much out of the reach of a child, a animal or a crop. Ask ICAT before mixing, and ask which product is actually on the list rather than the label.

per_item.reference: The symptoms point to cassava mosaic disease because the leaf deformation is the key tell, while the brown root rot belongs to cassava brown streak disease. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted cassava plants. Then, for the next sowing, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and avoid any mottled or deformed stems. After that, plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and maintain a uniform, well-fed stand. Finally, do not move cuttings from any affected area. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: My field shows cassava leaves that are yellow and twisted, but I also notice some brown rot in the roots. Which disease am I dealing with?

draws.answer: You are dealing with cassava mosaic disease in your cassava. Start by uprooting and destroying the strongly mottled, stunted cassava plants because they will not recover and they keep feeding the whitefly that spreads the virus. Then, in the next planting, take cuttings only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Next, plant an improved tolerant cassava variety obtained from ITRA or a certified cutting producer and maintain a uniform, well-fed cassava stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, go to ITRA.

Those signs are caused by cassava mosaic disease and brown rosette, not by cassava bacterial blight. First, pull out the plants that are strongly mottled, stunted, and have yellow or pale mottling and pull them out and destroy them. Then, for the next planting, cut only from plants that look healthy, with normal green leaves and no deformation. Do not cut from any mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you see angular spots with wilting instead of these signs, see ICAT; for clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: Striga hermonthica is the witchweed that appears as a purple/pink flowered weed at the base of stunted sorghum. Pull the weed by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted material so the seed does not spread. Apply organic manure together with a small amount of urea to the soil to weaken the parasite and strengthen the crop. Earth up the soil after fertilising. Rotate or intercrop with a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For badly infested fields, go to ICAT for tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: What steps should I take to manage Striga hermonthica in my sorghum crop?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is called groundnut on its own, so treat it as groundnut. Do not grow groundnut on the same land two years running; rotate with cereals instead. At ear level sow a regular groundnut variety and weed early about two weeks after sowing. Later apply the DFT-treatment seed to avoid the flower buds from being damaged. For a variety check and the exact product to use, see ICAT.

Striga hermonica is the common name for the parasitic plant Striga, so you must not grow sorghum on the same plot for more than two consecutive years, which limits the parasite. First, sow a sorghum field and perform the first weeding as scheduled. Second, at panicle initiation, take a pinch of groundnut, cotton or soya seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay 1 to 2 weeks after sowing and hold off any application beyond that time. Third, pull out any striga plants you notice and plant an extra-early sorghum or a mixed variety to keep the striga from returning. Fourth, ask ICAT for a striga-tolerant sorghum variety they recommend for the following season. ICAT is the service to contact.

per_item.reference: It is not nutrient deficiency, it is Striga, the parasitic weed that attaches to roots and robs the plant. Nutrient deficiency shows no attached weed, while Striga appears as a purple or pink-flowered weed clinging around the base of stunted plants. Because it is Striga, you must pull the weeds by hand before they flower and burn them to stop seed spread. After removal, add organic manure plus some urea, then earth up the soil. Finally, rotate or intercrop with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to reduce the seed bank. For tolerant varieties and a rotation plan, consult ICAT.

history.content: My sorghum has Striga, it must be nutrient deficiency, so I just add fertilizer

draws.answer: It is not Striga, it is a different thing. The two are told apart by where they come from: Striga is the parasitic plant that grows in the pocket between the plants, so the field is where it is, and it also makes a sticky substance that makes it stick up. Nutrient deficiency shows as uniform pale yellowing on older lower leaves with greener tops, no stalks, no worms, no spots, no root problem. Your sorghum shows those patterns. So the answer is to pull the striga plants out before they flower, not to add fertilizer. Also grow a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. ICAT for the striga plant and ITRA for the legume.

It is not nutrient deficiency, it is a parasitic infection. Striga is the parasite that grows on sorghum and takes host of the stem, so a fungicide will not work. Look for purple or pink clover-like flowers in the field; that is the sign of the parasite. Because it is a parasite, you must rogue out the worst-affected plants and destroy them, then use early weeding to keep weeds down. Use a tolerant variety for the next season. If you need help with the fungicide, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted weeds so the seed does not spread. history.content: I see a pink-flowered weed clinging to the base of my sorghum and the plants look short. What should I do?

draws.answer: Those weeds are a sign of striga in your sorghum field. Use a striga-tolerant sorghum variety and add a legume like groundnut, cowpea or soybean in rotation. Pull the striga plants out before they flower, using a strong stream or fire to destroy them. Make sure the plot is prepared before you start sowing the legume. For the right tolerant variety and advice on whether a fungicide is needed, go to ICAT.

The weed is causing striga in your sorghum and you need to rogue out or destroy the worst-affected plants to reduce the parasite. First, notice the purple or pink-flowered stigmas on the sorghum leaves, which indicate a strong striga plant. Then pull out the most infested sorghum plants and destroy them to eliminate the source of the pollen. After you remove the weeds, plant an improved striga-tolerant sorghum variety for the next season. Ask ICAT for a striga-tolerant variety and remove any weeds from the field.

per_item.reference: Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted weeds so the seed does not spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure plus some urea, which weakens Striga and strengthens your sorghum. Finally rotate or intercrop with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. These actions together reduce the seed that builds up in the soil. history.content: how stop Striga seed buildup

draws.answer: Rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source. Look under the rows at the soil surface every few weeks; if you see Striga with plants below two metres, pull them out and destroy them. Then keep the field free of weeds so the true plants have less neighbour-pollinator conflict. Sow an extra-early variety of 75 to 85 days, 2 to 3 seedlings per pocket, 10 to 15 plants per pocket at 50 x 50 cm. Plant the early variety in March in the southern zone or in May-June in the northern zone after a heavy rain, and weed around two weeks after sowing. For a variety that fits your region and season, see ICAT.

Do not grow cassava, cowpea, groundnut or cassava in the same field; rotate with maize. Plant a cereal after the cassava is cut so the nitrogen-fixing root nodules stay in the soil. Cut the stems at ground level so the nodules remain in the soil. Plant a cereal in the same plot to use the nitrogen. If you need a tolerant variety, see ITRA.

per_item.reference: Remove the pink-flowered weed by hand before it can flower and burn the removed material to stop seed spread. Then apply organic manure together with a little urea and earth up the soil to weaken the weed and improve your sorghum. Follow with a rotation or intercrop of a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to lower the seed bank. For a longer-term plan, see ICAT for tolerant sorghum varieties and a multi-year rotation strategy for badly infested fields.

history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink-flowered weed at the base, how can I manage it?

draws.answer: You say your sorghum is very stunted and you see a pink-flowered weed at the base. This sorghum problem is not something I was taught, and I will not guess a cause, a pest, a product or a dose because a wrong name could mislead you and a wrong dose could harm your crop or you and your family. The steps I can give you are to examine the sorghum closely, note which parts of the plants are affected, whether the symptoms started in one spot or all over, and whether they appeared after rain, a dry spell or any treatment. Pull one affected sorghum plant with its roots, keep it in a bag with a few leaves and do not spray anything until someone has seen it. Take the sample and your notes to the ICAT extension agent who can look at the field.

The problem is sorghum streak virus on your sorghum. First, walk the sorghum rows and look for a strong weevil attack that creates window-pane holes in the whorl leaves. Then pull out and destroy the most badly attacked sorghum plants to remove the source of the virus. After the field is cleared, use an improved sorghum variety that is tolerant to sorghum streak virus. For the following season, ask ICAT for a sorghum variety that matches the cycle and the grain colour you prefer. If a large share of your sorghum is affected, go to ICAT to confirm the disease and to obtain the tolerant variety.

per_item.reference: No, do not mix two products to make the spray stronger. Mixing chemicals that are not meant to go together can make a spray that burns your plants, harms your health, or simply does not work, and a stronger dose is not a better one. Use one approved product at a time, at the dose written on its label. If one product did not stop the pests, the problem may be the timing or the wrong product for that insect, not the strength. Ask ICAT which approved product fits the pest you see and when to spray it.

history.content: Would mixing two different insecticides give a stronger spray?

draws.answer: No, and the brochure says plainly that mixing two or more products does not make it work. Its own rule is that the product is chosen on the insecticide label and applied at the rate given for that product, not on a guess about how strong the mix is. Mixing is exactly what it warns against when it says to control them using several methods at once, which includes using a resistant variety, planting a tolerant variety, using an approved product at the labelled rate and keeping the field clean. If you need the product and its rate, take it to ICAT.

No, and mixing is not what the label says. What it says is to treat from a composition named: caustic soda at 1 percent, a formol solution at 10 percent, a quick oil, or a suitable insecticide at 50 to 100 grams per kilogram of grain. The order matters as much as the product, so treat one component at a time and never more. That is also why the guidance on grain protectant and fumigant is that of a product rather than of what to do with it.

per_item.reference: You need to vaccinate the healthy goats and sheep with the PPR vaccine after you isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. First, isolate every sheep or goat that has fever, muco-purulent discharge, mouth sores, diarrhoea, coughing or pneumonia. Then seal the herd by stopping any movement of animals in or out. Do not sell or slaughter any animal for market and dispose of any dead animals safely. Give the sick animals clean water and soft feed. After these measures, on veterinary advice give the PPR vaccine to all healthy and in-contact goats and sheep. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My sheep are dying fast from a disease that looks like PPR, what steps save the rest?

draws.answer: It is not gall sickness, it is leucaena poisoning from giving leucaena as the main feed. Reduce leucaena to a supplement, using only a quarter to a third of the ration at all. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal residues so the rumen has plenty of roughage. Introduce any feed change gradually over several days. Make sure the sheep always have clean water and a mineral or salt source. If appetite does not recover, call the veterinary service.

It is leucaena poisoning, not redwater. Reduce leucaena in the ration to only a quarter to a third and never make it the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen gets enough roughage. Change the feed gradually over several days and always provide clean water and a mineral or salt source. If appetite does not return or you see drooling or throat swelling, see the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Support the sick goats and sheep with water and soft feed. Do not sell or slaughter any animals during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Vaccinate the healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine, but only after veterinary advice. I cannot give you the exact date of the next vaccination campaign, and you should ask the veterinary service for that information.

history.content: When will the next PPR vaccination campaign start in my district

draws.answer: The next vaccination campaign against fowl pox is recommended for all adult birds, especially those that are vigorous and in good condition. You should first isolate any birds that show raised wart-like scabs on the comb, wattles or face. While the mild dry form runs its course you must give the isolated birds extra feed and fresh water while the mild dry form passes. Reduce mosquito numbers by clearing standing water and keeping the surroundings tidy. Then vaccinate the whole flock against fowl pox. I cannot give you the exact date for the next vaccination. For the precise timing, contact the veterinary service.

You should vaccinate your pigs against African swine fever as soon as you see any sick animals. First, confine all your pigs and stop any movement of pigs on or off the place. Second, keep all outside visitors away from the pen. Third, disinfect the pen and install a footbath at the entrance. Fourth, boil any food scraps before feeding them to the pigs. Fifth, dispose of dead pigs by burying or burning them and never sell or eat a sick pig. I cannot give you the exact date for the next vaccination campaign. For emergency assistance, see the veterinary service immediately.

per_item.reference: Uproot the pink-flowered plant by hand before it flowers and burn it to prevent its seeds from spreading. Apply organic manure together with a little urea to the soil to weaken the weed and boost sorghum growth. Follow this by rotating or intercropping with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to reduce the seed bank. For heavily infested fields you should see ICAT for tolerant sorghum varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: My sorghum is stunted and I notice a pink-flowered plant wrapping its stems near the ground. How can I manage this?

draws.answer: You are dealing with a severe sorghum stalk borer problem on your sorghum. While the sorghum is still young, add a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel; one kilogram covers about 1,500-2,000 plants. Do not use neem powder by itself because the oil will scorch the sorghum seedlings. After the sorghum is harvested, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop the field with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

The problem is from the thrips, pod borers and aphids that attack sorghum during flowering. Plant a resistant sorghum variety that matures in 55 to 75 days when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. About two weeks after sowing, do the first weeding to keep the field clean. Later, at the tillering stage, spray an approved product at the labelled rate. About ten days after the spray, apply the second application of the same product, and repeat the application ten days after the second. The approved product and exact dose can be obtained from ICAT.

per_item.reference: Those symptoms point to PPR, peste des petits ruminants, a fast and highly contagious virus affecting goats. First, isolate every sick goat together and halt all animal movements into or out of the herd. You must not sell or slaughter any goats for market during this outbreak, and any carcasses must be disposed of safely. Provide the sick goats with water and soft feed to support them. After that, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact goats with the PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: All my goats are running a fever, their eyes and noses are full of pus, and a few have died already.

draws.answer: Your goats are dealing with a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, carried by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. You should call the veterinary service the same day because only they can tell which disease it is and supply the correct drug and dose. Inform the vet about the urine colour: red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick every tick you can see on all your goats, not only on the sick one. Do not use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service will provide the needed treatment.

That is leucaena poisoning, not a tick-borne disease. Cut the leucaena back so it is only a quarter to a third of the ration and never the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen enough roughage. Change the feed gradually over several days and always provide clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the fever, swollen throat or drooling appear, see the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: Use organic manure together with some urea to weaken Striga and strengthen your sorghum, then earth up the field. After that, pull any Striga weeds by hand before they flower and burn them to prevent seed spread. Rotate or intercrop with a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank.

history.content: How much urea should I mix with manure to control Striga on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Use a rotation that includes a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. First, create a pocket 5 to 10 cm apart in each 20 x 20 cm pocket, placing 2 to 3 grains per pocket at a depth of 3 to 5 cm. After the crop, about a week later, drop a pinch of urea per pocket of your enriched soil. One pocket can hold roughly 100 kg of the mix, which is enough for about 5,000 to 6,500 plants. Avoid a first weeding of the field after the pinch. For a suitable pocket location and exact fertilizer rate, consult ICAT.

You should first raise a striga tolerant sorghum variety and rotate with a grain legume such as groundnut, cowpea or soybean, then cut the striga stems at ground level. After the crop, dry the striga-fast groundnut or cowpea leaves hard to about 13-14% moisture and toss them into a mouthful of soiled ash or oil to break the Ccurl, then pull the weeds at harvest. I cannot give you the exact amount of urea to mix with the manure, and the ICAT/ITRA agronomy service can advise you on the specific product details.

per_item.reference: The twisted leaves indicate cassava mosaic disease, while the brown corky rot inside the roots points to cassava brown streak disease. For the cassava mosaic disease plants, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted ones. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava mosaic disease plants and never from a deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. For the cassava brown streak disease plants, use cuttings only from healthy plants and a tolerant variety, then uproot and destroy the affected plants, avoiding any cuttings from that area. See ITRA for confirmation of both diseases and to obtain clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: My field has some cassava with twisted leaves and others with brown rot inside the roots. Which problem am I dealing with?

draws.answer: I cannot tell you which problem it is, and I do not want to say one of my two possibilities. Two of the eight cassava problems I hold describe cassava mosaic, leaf deformation and poor yield, and none of them says which of the four you are dealing with: twisted, puckered or shrunken leaves, brown or yellow mottling, or root or stem die-back. A soil organism can also show those signs, which is why no spray cures an infected plant. What I can do is tell you what each of them costs you. Tell me which of the four you are actually seeing, and I will show you what it costs you.

Cassava mosaic disease, also called cassava browning, is present in your cassava. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted cassava plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. When you plant again, take cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Use an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed cassava stand. If the symptoms are angular spots with wilting instead of leaf deformation, you should go to ICAT. For clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the service to see. I cannot give you any other service details.

Then spread organic manure mixed with a little urea over the soil to make conditions harder for Striga and help your sorghum grow. After cleaning the field, sow a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean together with sorghum to lower the seed bank. If the infestation is strong, visit ICAT for tolerant sorghum varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: I found a pink flower weed hugging the bottom of my short sorghum stalks, what steps should I take?

draws.answer: You are dealing with a stalk borer on your sorghum. While the sorghum is still young, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel. One kilogram of this mixture will treat roughly 1,500 to 2,000 plants, and you must repeat the application every 8 to 10 days. Always combine the pinch with the inert carrier because neem alone will scorch the plant. After the sorghum harvest, destroy or deep-bury the residues and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. Should a large area be attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control. I cannot provide a specific date for the first pinch.

The pink flower weed hugging the bottom of your short sorghum stalks is a sign of striga in the field. Pull out the most affected plants and destroy them to remove the source of the virus. After that, plan to use a striga tolerant sorghum variety for the next season. Remember that no spray will cure the infection. Contact ICAT to confirm striga and to obtain a tolerant variety recommendation.

Then feed the soil with organic manure and a little urea and earth up to weaken the weed and strengthen the sorghum. Next, rotate or intercrop the sorghum with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For tolerant sorghum varieties or a multi-year rotation plan, see ICAT.

history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink weed clinging to its base, how can I fix this?

draws.answer: You say the sorghum is very stunted and you see pink weed clinging to its base. This crop problem is not something I was taught, and I will not guess a cause, pest, disease, product or dose because a wrong name could mislead you. I recommend you walk the field, look at the plants, note which parts are affected, how many are impacted, whether the issue started in one area or across the whole plot, and whether it follows low ground or field edges. Pull one affected plant with its roots, keep it in a bag with a few leaves, and do not apply any spray until someone has examined it. Take the sample and your notes to the ICAT extension agent for further help.

The problem is stem borer on sorghum and you must use ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay. Drop a pinch of this mixture into each funnel of the young sorghum plants. One kilogram of the mixture will treat roughly 1,500 to 2,000 plants, so measure accordingly. Apply the pinch to every funnel and repeat the treatment every 8 to 10 days while the sorghum is still young and before flowering. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the sorghum. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the sorghum residues and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

On veterinary advice, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: How do I manage an outbreak of peste des petits ruminants in my flock?

draws.answer: Peste des petits ruminants is the everyday name for fowl pox in your cattle. First isolate the affected cattle from the rest of the herd. While they are isolated give them extra feed and fresh water as the disease runs its course. Remove standing water and keep the area around the cattle tidy to cut down mosquitoes. Then vaccinate the whole herd to prevent further infection. If you see any wet form with mouth or throat lesions, see the veterinary service.

The disease is called nagana, which is a trypanosomiasis of the red blood cells transmitted by tsetse flies. Keep all your cattle well fed and watered so they stay strong and can recover. Limit fly exposure by not grazing in riverine bush during the biting hours and consider fly control measures. Then report the case to the veterinary service for a professional diagnosis and the right trypanocide.

per_item.reference: No, brown corky rot inside the roots is a sign of cassava brown streak disease, not bacterial blight. Use cuttings only from plants that do not show yellow blotches along the leaf veins. Plant a tolerant cassava variety for the next cycle. Uproot and destroy any plant that shows the leaf symptoms and be careful not to carry cuttings from those fields. For verification you should see ITRA, because the disease is not well documented in Togo and root symptoms need checking. The disease is mainly reported in East Africa.

history.content: My cassava roots look brown and corky when I harvest them, could it be the same as bacterial blight?

draws.answer: The brown corky rot on cassava roots indicates cassava bacterial blight, not root rot. Use only healthy cuttings that have no gum, leaf deformation, or gum. Pull out and destroy every cassava plant showing those symptoms. Clean each cassava with a disinfectant before you plant the next crop. Choose a cassava variety that is known to withstand cassava bacterial blight and rotate the plot. You should see an ITRA representative or a registered producer for clean resistant cuttings.

Those signs indicate cassava bacterial blight, not cassava root or stem borer. When you cut the cassava stems, keep the corky rot inside the stem. Pull out and destroy the cassava plants that are affected. After each plant, clean and disinfect your cutting tools before you work on the next one. Then choose a resistant cassava variety and rotate the field to a different location. If you need clean resistant cuttings, you should go to ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the disease.

history.content: Can I mix two insecticides in one spray to make it stronger?

draws.answer: No, you cannot mix insecticides in a spray, because the product is not a blend but a product and the strength is fixed. The ITRA and ICAT brochure states this clearly: it says the product is chosen separately, for the insect on your plant, and it gives the product name and its rate from that name, not a concentration invented by mixing. So what you are doing is inventing a number, and the number comes out from a name rather than from a concentration. Ask ICAT, which holds the approved products and their rates. What I will not do is give you the mix; I will not invent it.

No, and a stronger mix does not treat the pest better. What the label says is that the product is an approved product, and that to use it you must read the label and not go beyond it, which is the whole point of the label. Among those four the product is a fungicide, an insecticide and a gas insecticide, and only the approved ones, so the label names the three, each with its own name and its rate per kilogram. What raises a product is the product itself, which is a product made of ingredients you can identify, and what goes wrong when you put two of those next to each other is that the two products are not meant to meet the same problem, so they fight each other. If it is what is bothering your crop, ask ICAT, who can see the plants and tell you what the problem is and whether a mix is the answer.

per_item.reference: These are signs of peste des petits ruminants in goats. Separate every sick goat at once and halt any movement of animals in or out of your herd. See an ITRA representative or a registered cutting producer for clean resistant cuttings.

history.content: my sorghum looks yellow because of nutrient deficiency, right?

draws.answer: Yes, the uniform pale yellowing of the older lower leaves while the young leaves stay green signals nitrogen shortage on a depleted soil. First, recognise that this is a nitrogen hunger problem, not a disease. Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word because mineral fertilizer alone often gives no return on run-down soil. Restore organic matter by applying manure, compost, or burying residues instead of burning them. Plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, see ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your field.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: You are facing leucaena poisoning in your goats caused by feeding leucaena as the main feed. Reduce the amount of leucaena to only a quarter to a third of the total ration and do not let it be the main feed. Blend the leucaena with grasses and cereal residues so the rumen receives enough roughage. Introduce any feed mix gradually over several days. Make sure the animals always have clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the appetite does not recover or you still see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, go to the veterinary service.

history.content: My goats are dying fast, they have fever, runny eyes and noses, and some have mouth sores, what is the problem?

draws.answer: Your goats are suffering from a tick-borne disease of cattle, either gall sickness or redwater, transmitted by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus. Contact the veterinary service immediately so they can identify whether it is gall sickness or redwater and supply the correct drug and dose. Inform the vet about the urine colour because red to black points to redwater and yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick goat in the shade, ensure clean water is available, and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not only on the sick goat. Only the veterinary service can provide the proper medication.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed attacking sorghum. Plant a legume such as cowpea or groundnut in the rotation and cut the legume stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Then pull out any weeds that appear on the sorghum and have them buried. After the legume is in the field, sow a grain or soya variety at the close spacing that would be used without the legume. Do not grow sorghum on the same plot for more than two consecutive years, which helps keep parasite pressure low. For a legume recommendation that fits your scheme, see ICAT.

Striga hermontha, also called sorghum stalk borer, is the caterpillar problem. While the sorghum plants are still young, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel; this treats about 1,500-2,000 plants per kilogram. One kilogram of the mixture will cover roughly 1,500-2,000 plants and you need to repeat the application every 8-10 days. Do not use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the sorghum. After the harvest, destroy or deep-bury the sorghum residues and plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean. For a large block of sorghum, go to ICAT for resistant varieties.
